Module 6›Chapter 5.5›Initial APIC Setup

Initial APIC Setup

Configuring Out-of-Band Management

Core Concept

Out-of-Band Management (OOB)

A dedicated network path for managing network devices, independent of the data plane. It's crucial for initial setup, troubleshooting, and maintaining access during fabric issues.

Key Parameters
  • IP Address: Unique identifier for the APIC on the OOB network.
  • Subnet Mask: Defines the network portion of the IP address.
  • Default Gateway: Route for traffic outside the local OOB subnet.
  • DNS Servers: For name resolution of external services.
Key Takeaway

Proper OOB configuration is the foundational step for APIC management and cluster formation, ensuring reliable access and communication.

APIC Console Setup

Power On APIC

Configure OOB IP, Subnet, Gateway, DNS via console.

Step 1
Common Mistake

Misconfiguring OOB IP settings (IP, mask, gateway) will prevent initial access and cluster formation. Always double-check these critical parameters.

screens.title: APIC Cluster Formation
screens.narratorSegment: Once your initial APIC is configured with its out-of-band management settings, the next critical step is forming the APIC cluster. This is not just an optional feature; it's fundamental for achieving high availability and redundancy in your ACI fabric. You'll typically deploy three, five, or even seven APIC controllers to form this cluster, ensuring that if one controller fails, the others can seamlessly take over management responsibilities. During the initial setup of the first APIC, you'll define key fabric-wide parameters, such as the fabric name, the TEP, or Tunnel Endpoint, pool for the overlay network, and the total size of your APIC cluster. Subsequent APICs are then added to this pre-defined cluster. Each APIC discovers its peers and establishes secure communication channels over their OOB interfaces. It's absolutely vital that all APICs in the cluster are running the same software version and have stable network connectivity on their OOB interfaces. A common mistake here is misconfiguring IP addresses or network settings, which can prevent APICs from discovering each other and forming a healthy, operational cluster. Always double-check your IP addresses, subnet masks, and gateway settings to avoid these issues.

screens.title: Fabric Discovery with LLDP
screens.narratorSegment: With the APIC cluster up and running, the next major phase is fabric discovery. This is where the APICs identify and register the physical leaf and spine switches that form the backbone of your ACI network. The APICs, which are connected to the leaf switches via their in-band management interfaces, utilize a crucial Layer 2 protocol called LLDP, or Link Layer Discovery Protocol, to discover these connected switches. When a leaf or spine switch powers on and connects to an APIC-managed fabric, it automatically sends out LLDP messages. The APIC receives these messages, processes the information, and identifies the switch. This then prompts the administrator to register the newly discovered switch within the APIC GUI. This automated discovery process significantly simplifies the initial setup, as you don't have to manually configure each switch individually. LLDP acts as the eyes and ears of the APIC, allowing it to build a comprehensive inventory of the physical fabric components. Module 6›Chapter 5.5›Fabric Discovery with LLDP

Fabric Discovery with LLDP

How APIC Finds Leaf and Spine Switches

Core Protocol

Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)

A vendor-neutral Layer 2 protocol used by network devices to advertise their identity, capabilities, and neighbors on a local area network. In ACI, it's key for APIC to discover switches.

Discovery Process
  • Leaf/spine switches power on and connect to the fabric.
  • They send LLDP messages advertising their presence.
  • APIC receives LLDP, identifies the switch, and prompts for registration.
  • Administrator assigns unique Fabric ID and Node ID.
Key Takeaway

LLDP is the fundamental mechanism for APIC to automatically discover and inventory physical leaf and spine switches, simplifying initial fabric setup.

LLDP Flow
APIC Controller
Receives LLDP
Leaf/Spine Switch
Sends LLDP

screens.title: Registering and Configuring Switches
screens.narratorSegment: After the APIC discovers the leaf and spine switches through LLDP, the next step is to register them and bring them under APIC's centralized management. As an administrator, you'll assign a unique fabric ID and a node ID to each discovered switch. This identification is crucial for the APIC to maintain an accurate inventory and apply policies correctly. Once registered, the APIC automatically pushes the initial configuration to these switches. This isn't just a basic setup; it includes assigning them their specific roles, whether they are a leaf switch connecting to endpoints or a spine switch forming the fabric's backbone. The APIC also configures the underlying routing protocols, such as IS-IS, that establish the physical connectivity backbone of the ACI fabric. This automated configuration push ensures consistency and adherence to the defined policies across all fabric switches, significantly reducing manual configuration errors and accelerating deployment. It's a powerful demonstration of ACI's policy-driven automation. screens.title: Understanding Fabric Access Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Once your ACI fabric is discovered and registered, the next crucial step is to configure fabric access policies. These policies are absolutely essential because they define how external devices, such as physical servers, firewalls, or hypervisors, connect to and interact with your ACI leaf switches. Think of them as the rules that bridge your physical infrastructure with the logical, policy-driven world of ACI. Without correctly configured access policies, the ACI fabric simply won't know how to handle traffic from devices connected to its ports. This can lead to connectivity issues, incorrect VLAN tagging, or even complete communication failures for your applications. Fabric access policies are a chain of interconnected components that ensure when an Endpoint Group, or EPG, is deployed and mapped to a VLAN, the correct physical port configuration is automatically applied. They are the glue that connects your physical world to the ACI virtual network. Module 6›Chapter 5.5›Fabric Access Policies

Understanding Fabric Access Policies

Connecting External Devices to ACI

Definition

Fabric Access Policies

A set of policies in ACI that define how external devices connect to the leaf switches. They map logical ACI constructs (EPGs, VLANs) to physical port configurations.

Why They Are Necessary
  • Integrate physical servers, firewalls, and hypervisors.
  • Ensure correct VLAN tagging and network segmentation.
  • Automate port configuration based on policy.
  • Prevent connectivity issues for applications.
Key Takeaway

Fabric Access Policies are the critical link between the physical network infrastructure and ACI's logical policy model, enabling seamless external device connectivity.

Policy Components
Physical Domains
VLAN Pools
Interface Policies

screens.title: Physical Domains and VLAN Pools
screens.narratorSegment: Let's dive into the first two key components of fabric access policies: Physical Domains and VLAN Pools. Physical Domains are essentially logical groupings of your physical infrastructure. For example, you might create a 'physical domain for servers' or a 'physical domain for firewalls.' These domains help categorize the types of devices that will connect to your ACI fabric, allowing you to apply consistent policies to similar infrastructure. Think of it as organizing your physical assets into logical buckets. Complementing this are VLAN Pools, which are ranges of VLAN IDs that can be used for encapsulation on access ports. Instead of manually assigning individual VLANs, you define a pool, and ACI dynamically allocates VLANs from this pool as needed. For instance, you might have a 'VLAN pool for production servers' with IDs 100-200. These two components work together to provide a structured way to manage both the physical connections and the network segmentation for your external devices. content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 5.5›Physical Domains & VLAN Pools

Physical Domains and VLAN Pools

Categorizing Infrastructure and Resources

Component 1

Physical Domains

Logical groupings of physical infrastructure components (e.g., bare-metal servers, firewalls) that connect to the ACI fabric. They help categorize and apply consistent policies to similar device types.

Example: phys_domain_servers, phys_domain_firewalls
Component 2

VLAN Pools

Ranges of VLAN IDs reserved for use by specific physical or virtual domains within the ACI fabric. These pools allow ACI to dynamically assign VLANs to endpoints as needed.

Example: vlan_pool_prod_servers (VLANs 100-200)
Key Takeaway

Physical Domains and VLAN Pools establish the foundational categorization and resource allocation for external device connectivity within the ACI fabric.

Categorization Flow
Physical Domain (e.g., Servers)
VLAN Pool (e.g., 100-200)
Managed Access

screens.title: AAEPs and Interface Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Building on Physical Domains and VLAN Pools, the next critical components in fabric access policies are Attachable Access Entity Profiles, or AAEPs, and Interface Policies. An AAEP acts as a crucial link; it connects VLAN pools to physical domains and also associates them with specific interface policies. Think of the AAEP as the bridge that tells ACI, 'For this type of physical infrastructure, use these VLANs and apply these physical port settings.' screens.narratorSegment: The final pieces of the fabric access policy puzzle are Interface Policy Groups and Port Selectors. Interface Policy Groups allow you to bundle similar interface policies together. For instance, you might create a group called 'Server Access Group' that includes policies for 10Gbps speed, LLDP enabled, and a specific CDP setting. screens.title: OOB Management for Fabric Switches
screens.narratorSegment: While the APIC manages the ACI fabric in-band, having a separate out-of-band, or OOB, network for the APICs and the leaf and spine switches themselves provides a critical lifeline. screens.title: Simulating Initial APIC OOB Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a conceptual simulation of the initial APIC out-of-band configuration, as if you were connected to the APIC's console. This activity highlights the critical steps and parameters you'll encounter. First, you'd connect a console cable to the APIC's console port and use a terminal emulator to access the CLI. The APIC will typically boot into an initial setup wizard, prompting you for essential information. You'll define the fabric name, assign a unique APIC ID, specify the number of APICs in your cluster, and give the controller a name. Crucially, you'll input the out-of-band management IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway, along with DNS server IP addresses. After setting a strong admin password and completing the wizard, the next step is verification. You'd attempt to ping the default gateway from the APIC CLI to confirm OOB connectivity. Finally, from your workstation, you'd try to access the APIC GUI using the configured OOB IP address via HTTPS. Remember, common mistakes include incorrect IP settings or duplicate IPs, which can prevent OOB access and cluster formation. Always double-check your entries.

Once your initial APIC is configured with its out-of-band management settings, the next critical step is forming the APIC cluster. This is not just an optional feature; it's fundamental for achieving high availability and redundancy in your ACI fabric. You'll typically deploy three, five, or even seven APIC controllers to form this cluster, ensuring that if one controller fails, the others can seamlessly take over management responsibilities. During the initial setup of the first APIC, you'll define key fabric-wide parameters, such as the fabric name, the TEP, or Tunnel Endpoint, pool for the overlay network, and the total size of your APIC cluster. This is where the APICs identify and register the physical leaf and spine switches that form the backbone of your ACI network. The APICs, which are connected to the leaf switches via their in-band management interfaces, utilize a crucial Layer 2 protocol called LLDP, or Link Layer Discovery Protocol, to discover these connected switches. When a leaf or spine switch powers on and connects to an APIC-managed fabric, it automatically sends out LLDP messages. The APIC receives these messages, processes the information, and identifies the switch. This then prompts the administrator to register the newly discovered switch within the APIC GUI. The final pieces of the fabric access policy puzzle are Interface Policy Groups and Port Selectors. Interface Policy Groups allow you to bundle similar interface policies together. For instance, you might create a group called 'Server Access Group' that includes policies for 10Gbps speed, LLDP enabled, and a specific CDP setting. This grouping simplifies management and ensures consistency across multiple ports that require the same configuration. Port Selectors, along with Access Port Selectors, are then used to apply these policy groups to specific ports or ranges of ports on your leaf switches. This is where the rubber meets the road, connecting the logical policies to the physical hardware. For example, to connect a bare-metal server, you would create a VLAN pool, an AAEP, an interface policy for the server port, an interface policy group, and then apply this group to the specific leaf switch port connected to the server using a port selector. This entire chain of access policies ensures that when an EPG is deployed and mapped to a VLAN from that VLAN pool, the correct physical port configuration is automatically applied, providing granular control and automation.

While the APIC manages the ACI fabric in-band, having a separate out-of-band, or OOB, network for the APICs and the leaf and spine switches themselves provides a critical lifeline. This dedicated OOB network is a safety net for troubleshooting or in case of any fabric-wide issues that might disrupt in-band management. Each APIC has its own dedicated OOB management ports, which we discussed configuring earlier. For the Nexus 9000 switches that form your fabric, you'll configure their dedicated management interfaces, typically labeled 'mgmt0', with IP addresses on your OOB network. This setup allows you to SSH directly into individual switches if needed, completely independent of the ACI fabric's operational status. Imagine a scenario where the in-band network is experiencing problems; your OOB access ensures you can still reach and diagnose the individual components. Setting up robust OOB access from the very beginning is a best practice that no data center administrator should ever overlook, as it provides invaluable resilience and diagnostic capability. Let's walk through a conceptual simulation of the initial APIC out-of-band configuration, as if you were connected to the APIC's console. This activity highlights the critical steps and parameters you'll encounter. First, you'd connect a console cable to the APIC's console port and use a terminal emulator to access the CLI. The APIC will typically boot into an initial setup wizard, prompting you for essential information. You'll define the fabric name, assign a unique APIC ID, specify the number of APICs in your cluster, and give the controller a name. Crucially, you'll input the out-of-band management IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway, along with DNS server IP addresses. After setting a strong admin password and completing the wizard, the next step is verification. You'd attempt to ping the default gateway from the APIC CLI to confirm OOB connectivity. Finally, from your workstation, you'd try to access the APIC GUI using the configured OOB IP address via HTTPS. Remember, common mistakes include incorrect IP settings or duplicate IPs, which can prevent OOB access and cluster formation. Always double-check your entries.

As we conclude this chapter, let's recap some of the most essential concepts that underpin basic ACI fabric setup and initial configuration. First, remember Out-of-Band Management, or OOB. This is your dedicated, independent network path for managing devices, crucial for initial setup and troubleshooting. It's the lifeline that ensures you can always reach your APICs and switches. Next, we have the APIC Cluster. This group of three or more APIC controllers works together to provide high availability and redundancy, ensuring your ACI fabric remains operational and manageable even if an individual controller fails. Finally, Fabric Discovery is the automated process by which APIC controllers identify and register the physical leaf and spine switches connected to the fabric. This process transforms raw hardware into managed network components, ready for policy enforcement. These three concepts are fundamental to bringing your ACI fabric to life.

Let's continue reinforcing our understanding with more key concepts from this chapter. LLDP, or Link Layer Discovery Protocol, is a critical Layer 2 protocol that enables network devices to advertise their identity and capabilities. In ACI, it's the primary mechanism for APICs to discover leaf and spine switches. Then we have Fabric Access Policies, which are a comprehensive set of rules defining how external devices connect to your ACI leaf switches. These policies are crucial for integrating physical infrastructure into the ACI logical model. Finally, a Physical Domain is a logical grouping of physical infrastructure components, such as bare-metal servers or firewalls, that connect to the ACI fabric. It helps categorize and apply consistent policies to similar types of external devices. Understanding these terms is vital for effectively deploying and managing your ACI environment.
